opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about it in a few layers, because "inference per dollar" is really the product of a bunch of different things stacked on top of each other.

At the bottom you have the hardware: how many FLOPs and how much memory bandwidth you get per dollar. That's largely set by the chip vendors, but it matters a lot which hardware you pick for which workload. Some workloads are compute-bound and some are memory-bound, and those want different things.

Then there's the kernel and systems layer, which is where I've spent a lot of my time. The question there is: given this hardware, how close to peak are you actually getting? For a long time the answer for a lot of inference workloads was "not very close." Attention, for example, was bottlenecked on memory movement, not compute, and that's what motivated FlashAttention. In decoding especially, you're often just reading the weights and the KV cache over and over, so you're memory-bandwidth bound. A lot of the wins come from fusing operations, avoiding unnecessary reads and writes, and batching well so you actually use the compute you're paying for.

Above that you have the serving and scheduling layer: continuous batching, how you manage the KV cache, paging, prefix caching, speculative decoding, how you split prefill and decode. These can give multiples of improvement without touching the model at all.

Then there's the model itself. Architecture choices matter enormously for inference cost. Quantization, mixture of experts, smaller models distilled from bigger ones, and architectures that don't have a KV cache growing linearly with context, like state space models or hybrids. That's part of why I've been excited about things like Mamba. If you change the architecture, you change the shape of the cost curve, not just the constant.

And finally there's the application and workload level: what you're actually serving. Long context, agents making many calls, reasoning models generating lots of tokens. The workload has shifted a lot toward generating many tokens, which makes decode efficiency even more important.

So I'd say the big lesson is that you don't get there by optimizing one layer in isolation. The biggest gains come from co-designing across layers: designing the architecture with the hardware in mind, writing kernels that match the model's structure, and building serving systems that match the workload. Each layer might give you 2x, but they multiply, and that's how you've seen inference costs drop by orders of magnitude over the last couple of years.

r002.rationale: It says architecture choices change inference costs, but does not identify architecture design as extracting more intelligence from the same computation.

r003.rationale: It explains that kernel and systems optimization can bring workloads closer to peak and better use the compute being paid for, improving effective FLOPs per dollar.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I like to think about it is that inference per dollar is really a product of a few things, and you want to attack each of them separately. The first is the hardware itself: what does a GPU cost you per hour, and how much of its peak capability are you actually using? Most people are surprised when they measure it, because real workloads often sit at a small fraction of peak FLOPs or peak memory bandwidth. So one big lever is just utilization, closing the gap between what the chip can do and what your software is getting out of it.

The second piece is understanding what the bottleneck actually is, because inference is really two different regimes. Prefill, when you're processing the prompt, is compute-bound, it looks a lot like training. Decode, when you're generating tokens one at a time, is memory-bound. You're loading all the weights and the KV cache from memory for every single token, and the arithmetic you do with them is tiny. So the metric you care about shifts. In prefill you're asking how many FLOPs per second you can sustain. In decode you're asking how many bytes you can move, and how many requests you can batch together so that each byte you load gets amortized across more tokens.

That leads to the third lever, which is batching and the KV cache. The more concurrent sequences you can serve at once, the better your arithmetic intensity gets, but you're limited by memory capacity, and the KV cache is what eats it. So a lot of the work I've been interested in, things like FlashAttention, Mamba, state space models, is really about shrinking or restructuring that memory footprint so you can fit more in flight. Fewer bytes per token means higher batch size means more tokens per second per dollar.

And then there's a whole set of algorithmic tricks that sit on top: quantization, speculative decoding, better scheduling, disaggregating prefill and decode onto different machines. Each one attacks a different term in that equation.

So when I break it down I'd say: figure out which regime you're in, measure how far you are from the roofline for that regime, and then ask whether the fix is at the kernel level, the memory level, or the architecture level. Usually the answer is all three, but you want to know which one is giving you the biggest multiplier right now.

r002.rationale: It mentions architecture ideas that reduce memory use and improve throughput, but does not say architecture can extract more intelligence from the same computation.

r003.rationale: It names kernel-level fixes and describes improving utilization by closing the gap between peak capability and software performance, which communicates kernel optimization as a way to improve effective FLOPs per dollar.

astra-6.text:
I’d break it down into three pieces: the model, the hardware, and the system that connects them. Ultimately, you want to serve as much useful work as possible for a given cost, while meeting your quality and latency requirements.

On the model side, can you get the quality you need with a smaller model or lower precision? On the hardware side, what are you paying for compute, memory capacity, and memory bandwidth? And then on the systems side, how much of that hardware are you actually using?

For language models, it helps to separate processing the prompt from generating the response. Processing the prompt tends to involve large matrix multiplications, so compute efficiency matters a lot. Generating tokens one at a time often puts more pressure on memory bandwidth: you’re reading a lot of model weights to do relatively little computation. Batching helps you reuse those weights across requests, but you have to balance that against latency and the memory needed for the KV cache.

So I wouldn’t optimize tokens per second in isolation. I’d ask: at the quality we need, and within the latency our users can tolerate, how many requests can we serve per dollar? Then we can identify which bottleneck is actually limiting us.

r002.rationale: It mentions smaller models and lower precision as ways to meet a quality target, but does not identify architecture design as extracting more intelligence from the same computation.

r003.rationale: The response discusses hardware utilization and bottlenecks, but does not identify kernel optimization as a way to improve FLOPs per dollar.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as two pieces: how much computation you need to get a useful answer, and how efficiently you execute that computation on the hardware. On the model side, that includes things like model size, precision, and how many tokens you generate. On the systems side, it’s how well you use the GPU—how much time you spend doing useful computation versus moving data or waiting.

And then you have to specify the constraints. Are you maximizing throughput, or do you need to respond within a certain latency? You can often get better throughput by batching more requests, but that can make individual users wait longer. So the goal is really to serve as many useful answers as possible per dollar, at the quality and latency that your application needs.
